stories.title: Haze Alert: Singapore's Air Turns Unhealthy
stories.headline_kid: The air in central Singapore turned unhealthy this morning because of smoke drifting in from nearby forest fires.
summary: Singapore uses a number called the PSI (Pollutant Standards Index) to tell people how clean or dirty the air is. Today, the PSI in central Singapore hit 101, which crosses into the 'unhealthy' zone. In other parts of the island, the air was still 'moderate', with readings between 74 and 87.
This haze is not made in Singapore. It comes from huge fires burning in Kalimantan, part of Indonesia, where smoke drifts across the sea on the wind and settles over Singapore and Malaysia.

When the air is unhealthy, it can make your throat feel scratchy, your eyes itchy, and breathing harder, especially if you run around outside. The National Environment Agency (NEA) is watching the air closely and may advise schools to reduce outdoor activities if things get worse.

Doctors suggest drinking more water, staying indoors when possible, and keeping windows closed. Young children and elderly people should be extra careful, since their lungs are more sensitive to smoky air.

lenses.me: If the PSI near you is high, you might feel your throat get scratchy or your eyes water when playing outside.
lenses.family: Your family might keep the windows shut and switch on an air purifier at home until the haze clears.
lenses.friends: Your outdoor PE lesson or recess time might move indoors if the haze gets worse at school.
lenses.nation: Singapore's NEA checks PSI levels in five regions every hour so the whole country can be warned early.
lenses.world: This shows how smoke from fires in one country can travel across the sea and affect the air that millions of people breathe in nearby countries.

stories.title: Malaysia Tries to Make It Rain to Fight the Haze
stories.headline_kid: Malaysia is sending planes to sprinkle special chemicals into clouds, hoping to make it rain and wash away thick haze.
summary: Cloud seeding is like giving clouds a little nudge. Planes fly up and drop tiny particles into clouds, which helps water droplets stick together and fall as rain faster than they normally would.

Malaysia started a three-day cloud-seeding operation this week because Sarawak state has been covered in thick, smoky haze for days. The smoke is drifting over from huge fires burning in Kalimantan, part of Indonesia, and it has made the air dangerous to breathe.
The rain-making mission has two goals: to clear the smoky skies, and to fill up water reservoirs behind three hydroelectric dams before the dry season makes water scarce.
This haze doesn't stay in one place — the same smoke that is choking Sarawak also drifts towards Singapore and other parts of Malaysia, which is why the whole region is hoping the rain-making works.

lenses.me: If it rains in the region, the smoky smell and hazy skies you sometimes notice from your window could clear up faster.
lenses.family: Your family might check haze and air quality apps just like families in Sarawak do right now.
lenses.friends: Friends with relatives in Malaysia might tell you that outdoor school activities there have been cancelled.
lenses.nation: Singapore watches the very same haze source, and could use similar rain-making tools if our air ever gets much worse.
lenses.world: This shows how neighbouring countries sometimes need to team up and use clever tools to solve pollution problems that cross borders.

stories.title: Can ASEAN Ever Beat the Haze for Good?
stories.headline_kid: Malaysia wants Southeast Asian countries to work harder together to stop haze — but it's not easy.
summary: More than 20 years ago, Southeast Asian countries signed a promise called the ASEAN Transboundary Haze Agreement, agreeing to stop smoke from fires crossing into each other's countries. ASEAN even set a goal to be completely haze-free by 2030.

But experts say this goal will be very hard to reach. The haze usually comes from people illegally burning forests and plantations in Indonesia to clear land cheaply and quickly for farming. Strong winds then carry the smoke across the sea to Malaysia, Singapore and beyond.

Malaysia is now pushing ASEAN to take tougher action, such as punishing companies and individuals responsible for starting fires. Without stronger enforcement, experts warn the same smoky problem will likely return every dry season.

Singapore has pushed for stronger haze laws for years too, since our air quality suffers whenever fires rage in neighbouring countries. A stronger regional agreement could mean fewer hazy days for everyone in the future.

lenses.me: Less haze in future could mean more days where you can play outside without worrying about your throat or eyes.
lenses.family: Cleaner regional air means fewer doctor visits for breathing problems in many families, not just yours.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose families travel to Malaysia or Indonesia would get to enjoy clearer holidays there.
lenses.nation: Singapore has long called for stronger haze rules, since our country also suffers when smoke drifts in from outside.
lenses.world: This shows how countries must cooperate and truly enforce shared rules to solve problems, like pollution, that don't stop at borders.

stories.title: Reaching Nepal's Flood Survivors Is 'Very, Very Difficult'
stories.headline_kid: A week after Nepal's terrible flood, helpers are struggling to reach villages cut off by broken roads and bridges.
summary: A huge chunk of glacier and mountain collapsed in Nepal, causing catastrophic flash floods that destroyed roads, bridges and even hydropower dams in the Himalayan region. More than a thousand people have died, and the disaster happened just over a week ago.
Now the United Nations says getting help to survivors is 'very, very difficult'. Whole communities near the disaster's centre are completely cut off, with no roads left to drive supplies in.

Aid workers are now considering unusual methods to reach these isolated villages — including cargo drones that can fly over broken roads, and porters who carry supplies on their backs through the mountains on foot.

Meanwhile, families of missing tourists, including foreigners, are still searching hospitals and morgues in Kathmandu for news of their loved ones. Singapore had earlier sent police search-and-rescue specialists to help, showing just how much support is still needed.

lenses.me: This story helps you understand how hard it is to get help to people when nature destroys the roads and bridges we normally rely on every day.
lenses.family: Your family might choose to donate to relief funds set up to help flood survivors rebuild their lives.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might talk about how new technology like drones can help save lives during disasters.
lenses.nation: Singapore sent rescue teams to Nepal earlier, showing how our country helps neighbours in the region during tough times.
lenses.world: This disaster shows how extreme weather can test how well countries and aid groups work together, especially in difficult mountain terrain.

stories.title: From Failing Every Subject to Fighting for Every Student
stories.headline_kid: Meet a Singapore teacher who once could not even read in Primary 1 — now she never gives up on students who are struggling.
summary: Raja Shahridah Raja Suhaini grew up in a poor family, could not read when she was in Primary 1, and failed almost every subject in school. She even says, 'I hated school.'

Today, she is a secondary school teacher, and she has just been named a National Level winner at the National Institute of Education's Caring Teacher Award 2026 — one of the highest honours a teacher in Singapore can receive.

What makes her special is how far she goes for her students. When students skip school, she personally knocks on their doors to check on them — even when those doors are sometimes slammed shut in her face.
Her own difficult childhood is exactly why she refuses to give up on any child. She believes every student, no matter how much they are struggling, deserves someone who won't stop believing in them.

lenses.me: Her story reminds you that struggling with schoolwork now doesn't mean you can't succeed later in life.
lenses.family: Parents can see how much a caring teacher's support matters for a child's confidence and future.
lenses.friends: Friends who find lessons difficult might feel encouraged knowing even a top award-winning teacher once failed almost everything.
lenses.nation: Singapore's Caring Teacher Award celebrates teachers who go far beyond lessons to truly look out for their students.
lenses.world: Her story is a reminder that kindness and never giving up can change a person's life, no matter where they grow up.
